q-83481.source_problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 9 & -7 \\ -14 & 13 & -8 \\ -2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$
q-83481.source_quote:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 9 & -7 \\ -14 & 13 & -8 \\ -2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-11 & 9 & -7 \\ -14 & 11 & -8 \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-11{x}_{1}+9{x}_{2}-7{x}_{3}=0 \\ -14{x}_{1}+11{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-11 & 9 & -7 & 0 \\ -14 & 11 & -8 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -14 & 11 & -8 & 0 \\ -11 & 9 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-7){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{11}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{7}{2} & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{7}{8}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

fields.binding: The source explicitly chooses the full eigenvector [1;2;1] for the requested eigenvalue 2.
fields.source_quote:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 9 & -7 \\ -14 & 13 & -8 \\ -2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-11 & 9 & -7 \\ -14 & 11 & -8 \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-11{x}_{1}+9{x}_{2}-7{x}_{3}=0 \\ -14{x}_{1}+11{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-11 & 9 & -7 & 0 \\ -14 & 11 & -8 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -14 & 11 & -8 & 0 \\ -11 & 9 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-7){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{11}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{7}{2} & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{7}{8}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

q-83505.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-83505.source_problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨8(1-2t)^{3},12(1+4t)^{2}⟩,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,-26⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
q-83505.source_quote:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨8(1-2t)^{3},12(1+4t)^{2}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 8(1-2t)^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 12(1+4t)^{2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-(1-2t)^{4}+{C}_{1},\,(1+4t)^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨-1,-26⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨-(1-2(0))^{4}+{C}_{1},\,(1+4(0))^{3}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-26⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-27.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨-(1-2t)^{4},\,(1+4t)^{3}-27⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨-(1-2t)^{4},\,(1+4t)^{3}-27⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}-(1-2t)^{4} & =0\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{2}, \\ (1+4t)^{3}-27 & =0\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=\frac{1}{2},$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

q-83826.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-83826.source_problem: According to the rational roots theorem, which of the following **cannot** be a root of the polynomial $f(x)=7{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x+6?$
q-83826.source_quote:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $6$ and the leading coefficient is $7.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }6}{\text{factor of }7}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $-7$ does not take the above form. The value $-7$ can be interpreted as a fraction $-\frac{7}{1},$ and the numerator $(7)$ is not a factor of $6.$

q-84598.source_problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
q-84598.source_quote:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda  & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

q-84829.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-84829.source_problem: What are the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola ${x}^{2}=12y?$
q-84829.source_quote:
The standard equation of an upward- or downward-opening parabola that has its vertex at the origin is

$$
{x}^{2}=4py,
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

We can rewrite the given equation as 

$$
{x}^{2}=4(3)y.
$$

It is now clear that our equation is of the standard type with $p=3.$ Therefore, our parabola has its vertex at $(0,0).$

q-85966.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-85966.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/8e03226558b1dbb2e93d23947b0b05f3d8413dc35207bbe9b536e68108f40955.png)

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing by $3\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ while the $5\,\text{cm}$ height does not change. If the volume of the rectangular prism is increasing at a rate of $15\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min},$  how fast is its width changing when its dimensions are $6\,\text{cm}$ in length and $2\,\text{cm}$ in width?
q-85966.source_quote:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =2\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =5\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-3\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =15\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=6\,\text{cm},$ $y=2\,\text{cm}$ and $z=5\,\text{cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Since $z$ is not changing and $z=5,$ we get

$$
V=5xy.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5xy) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =5x(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+5y(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =5(6)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+5(2)(-3) \\ 15 & =30(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})-30 \\ 45 & =30(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=6\,\text{cm},$ $y=2\,\text{cm}$ and $z=5\,\text{cm}.$

Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=5x+6y,\,y(0)=1
$$

Use Euler's method with one step to approximate $y(1).$
q-86975.source_quote:
Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=1,$ we will use a step size of 

$$
Δx=1-0=1.
$$

First, we add the initial condition data:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5x+6y \\  & =5\cdot (0)+6\cdot 1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $6$ |  |

Next, we compute $Δy$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(6)\cdot 1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $6$ | $6$ |

To get the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x$ and $Δy$ to $y,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =1+6 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these rows to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $6$ | $6$ |
| $1$ | $7$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈7.$

q-89417.source_problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$
q-89417.source_quote:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

q-89589.source_problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}$ for $s>4.$
q-89589.source_quote:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+L{-{e}^{4t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}} & =\frac{1}{s+2},\,s>-2 \\ L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)-(s+2)}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =\frac{-6}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =-\frac{6}{(s+2)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{-2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-2,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (4,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(-2,\infty )\cap (4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>4.$

fields.binding: The sole selection field requests the Laplace transform for the stipulated s>4; the saved transform calculation ends at -6/((s+2)(s-4)).
fields.source_quote:
Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)-(s+2)}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =\frac{-6}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =-\frac{6}{(s+2)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-94267.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-94267.source_problem: The function $y(t)$ gives the position of a particle at time $t.$ Which of the following equations represents a situation in which the particle is undergoing simple harmonic motion?
q-94267.source_quote:
The simple harmonic motion (SHM) equation is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.
$$

We can see that the only equation that represents SHM is

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{4}y=0.
$$

In the above case:

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\omega =\frac{1}{2}
$$

q-94283.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-94283.source_problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with simple harmonic motion, is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+8y=0,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with a velocity of $4\,\text{m/s},$ find the amplitude of the oscillation.
q-94283.source_quote:
The simple harmonic motion (SHM) equation is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.
$$

The general solution to the SHM equation can be written as

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ),
$$

where $R$ is the amplitude, and $ϕ$ is the phase. In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=8\,⟹\,\omega =2\sqrt{2}.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\sqrt{2}t+ϕ).
$$

We're given the initial condition $y(0)=0.$ Substituing this into the equation gives

$$
R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=0\,⟹\,ϕ=0.
$$

So our general solution reduces to

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\sqrt{2}t).
$$

We're told that the velocity is $4\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0,$ which means that ${y}^{′}(0)=4.$ Differentiating the general solution with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=2\sqrt{2}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{2}t).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=4$ into the above gives

$$
4=2\sqrt{2}R\,⟹\,R=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the amplitude is $\sqrt{2}\,\text{m}.$ The solution for $y(t)$ is

$$
y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\sqrt{2}t).
$$

q-94609.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-94609.source_problem: Find the center of the elliptic cone $4(x-1)^{2}+10(y-4)^{2}={z}^{2}.$
q-94609.source_quote:
The general equation of an elliptic cone with center at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=\frac{(z-{z}_{0})^{2}}{{c}^{2}}.
$$

To find the center, we rewrite our equation in standard form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}+10(y-4)^{2} & =(z-0)^{2} \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{1/10} & =(z-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic cone that has its center at $(1,4,0).$

q-95216.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-95216.source_problem: What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{6\times 4}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 4$ matrices over $R?$
q-95216.source_quote:
The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R)$ contains a total of $n\cdot m$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{3\times 2}(R)$ contains $3\cdot 2=6$ elements, and is given by

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{6\times 4}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{6\times 4}(R))=6\cdot 4=24.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R))=n\cdot m.
$$

q-96040.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-96040.source_problem:
Which of the following is the correct symbolic notation for the sentence given below?

*"The function $g$ maps the set $X$ to the set of real numbers."*
q-96040.source_quote:
The sentence *"The function $g$ maps the set $X$ to the set of real numbers"* is equivalent to the following symbolic notation:

$\,$ $g:X\to R$

Here, the domain of $g$ is $X,$ and the codomain of $g$ is $R.$

q-96231.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-96231.source_problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \,∗\, \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $U$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $U?$
q-96231.source_quote:
Recall that since $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ the matrix $U$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

q-97071.source_problem:
Let
$T=[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]$
be the standard matrix of the linear transformation $T.$ Then $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto
q-97071.source_quote:
Notice that $T$ has proportional rows, and yet $T$ is not the zero matrix. 

Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=1$ and $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line that passes through the origin.

Moreover, the line must pass through the origin $(0,0)$ and the points $(6,2)$ and $(9,3),$ which are defined by the columns of the matrix $T.$ 

Computing the slope $m$ of this line, we get

$$
m=\frac{3-2}{9-6}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

 

Therefore, $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $y=\frac{1}{3}x.$

q-98117.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-98117.source_problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where $a=⟨3,2,5⟩$ and $b=⟨1,4,1⟩$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(a)=2$ and $f(b)=3,$ then what is missing from the statement below?

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $\text{_______________}\,.$ *
q-98117.source_quote:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)\cdot (b-a) \\ 3-2 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c),{f}_{z}(c)⟩\cdot (⟨1,4,1⟩-⟨3,2,5⟩) \\ 1 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c),{f}_{z}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨-2,2,-4⟩ \\ 1 & =-2{f}_{x}(c)+2{f}_{y}(c)-4{f}_{z}(c) \\ -1 & =2{f}_{x}(c)-2{f}_{y}(c)+4{f}_{z}(c).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $2{f}_{x}(c)-2{f}_{y}(c)+4{f}_{z}(c)=-1.$ *

fields.source_quote:
Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $2{f}_{x}(c)-2{f}_{y}(c)+4{f}_{z}(c)=-1.$ *

q-98765.review_method: manual interpretation of saved MA solution and prompt role
q-98765.source_problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$
q-98765.source_quote:
Recall that if $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeros outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}+\frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]

q-98768.source_problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$
q-98768.source_quote:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}-\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{4}{5} & 0 & -\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & 0 & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]

q-99009.source_quote:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C \\  & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

fields.source_quote:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

q-99204.source_problem: Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the maximum product of three positive numbers given that the sum of their squares is $108.$
q-99204.source_quote:
Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be three positive numbers. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=108.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=108
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}yz=2\lambda x \\ xz=2\lambda y \\ xy=2\lambda z\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}xyz=2\lambda {x}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {y}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =108 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2} & =36 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(6,6,6),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(6,6,6)=6\cdot 6\cdot 6=216.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,2,2) & =10\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =40 \\  & <f(6,6,6).\end{aligned}
$$
